message.reasoning:
I am ready to play Monopoly and make a decision.

I am reviewing my holdings. I have $58 cash and all three pink properties are fully upgraded with three houses each. Most other properties remain mortgaged.

Opponent p2 has heavy cash and monopolies across light blues, reds, and dark blues. Opponent p4 is down to $279 after paying $600 on Boardwalk. My three-house pink properties now charge $450 each in rent.

Virginia Avenue now charges $500 in rent with three houses. Opponent p4 is on Boardwalk and will roll next. They may pass my pink properties after landing on GO.

A roll of 12 is needed to reach St. Charles from Boardwalk, so p4 will not land there immediately. I am weighing trade proposals, house sales, or ending the turn. I will avoid selling the three-house spike unless debt forces it, and I will not trade my pink properties, St. James Place, or Pennsylvania Avenue to p2.

Opponent p4 cannot afford to buy my mortgaged Pennsylvania Avenue. Trading with them is unlikely to help. I will not trade with p2 either, since that would strengthen their dark blue and red monopolies.

P2 is currently on New York Avenue. They have passed my pink properties for this lap and will return next turn.

I am calculating the exact spaces I will land on next turn. Income Tax is the biggest immediate threat, costing $200 and impossible to pay with only $58 cash. The other spaces are either harmless or already mortgaged.

I am calculating how to raise cash if I land on Income Tax. Selling one house from each pink property would yield $150, enough to cover the $200 tax with my $58 cash. I am also checking whether selling just one house for Reading Railroad is allowed under even-building rules.

Selling just one house from a property would leave an uneven distribution, so I must sell one house from each pink property. That would destroy the three-house spike and drop rent to roughly $150–180 per property.

I am now considering trading my mortgaged Pennsylvania Avenue to opponent p4 for cash. They currently refuse to pay the full $300 price while Pacific is unowned, but the mortgage value is only $160. I could offer a lower price to raise cash without selling houses and destroying my three-house spike.

I am now weighing whether to sell my mortgaged Connecticut Avenue. Opponent p4 does not need it, and they are too cash-poor to pay a fair price. I would rather keep it as a defensive blocker against p2 than give them a light-blue monopoly.

St. James Place is mortgaged and split across three players, so giving it to p4 would not complete a monopoly. The B&O Railroad is the only viable trade target; giving it to p4 would block p2 from doubling rent on their third railroad, and p4 might pay for that protection.

Dark blues are 36 spaces away, so they pose no immediate threat. I am now focusing on raising $50–150 from opponent p4 to survive the upcoming Income Tax and Reading Railroad without selling houses.

The mortgaged B&O Railroad is worth only about $100, so p4 would likely pay little for it. I am also reconsidering offering Pennsylvania Avenue for a lower price, though p4 may still refuse. I have ruled out trading Connecticut Avenue to p2; that would complete their light-blue monopoly and let them build faster.

I must not trade Connecticut Avenue to p2 before my next roll. They would build light blue houses and raise rent from $4–12 to $40–60. That would be catastrophic.

I also cannot give B&O Railroad to p2 now. That would let them double Reading Railroad rent from $100 to $200, compounding the Income Tax threat.

Opponent p4 cannot afford both Atlantic and Pacific, so they may land on one of them. I am now weighing whether they would pay for the B&O Railroad to block p2 from completing four railroads.

I am now considering a single trade proposal to opponent p4 rather than ending the turn immediately. I have enough cash to cover the upcoming tax and rent without selling houses, so trading carries little immediate need. I am weighing whether a smaller offer for the B&O Railroad might work, though p4 has been cash-conservative and previously rejected similar deals.

Opponent p4 will likely land on my pink properties within two turns. With $279 cash and a $200 GO bonus, they can afford the $500 Virginia rent but may bust there. If they go bankrupt, I would inherit their assets.

I have decided to end the turn without selling houses or trading. If opponent p4 lands on my pink properties and cannot pay, I would inherit their assets and cash. I will not offer them a "safe passage" deal.

Mortgaging is impossible because the mortgageable and unmortgageable lists are empty, and I lack the $66 to unmortgage Connecticut. Building is also blocked by insufficient cash or maxed even-building rules. The only remaining legal actions are ending the turn, proposing a trade, or selling houses. Selling houses would be wrong without debt, so a single low-risk trade proposal is preferable.

Opponent p4 cannot afford to buy my mortgaged Pennsylvania Avenue for $300. I am now considering offering it for only $100 as a cheap future asset, since they still need Pacific Avenue and may accept the low price.

A $100 offer for Pennsylvania Avenue would still leave me $42 short of the $200 Income Tax. I would have to sell houses anyway to cover that tax. The green lever is not worth that sacrifice. Opponent p4 could later monopolize the greens and challenge p2. That might be good or bad. Undeveloped green rent is low. I will not trade it.

I will not trade B&O Railroad to p4 for $50–80. That would let p2 double Reading Railroad rent and could be catastrophic if I roll a 4 next turn. I will also wait until after clearing the railroad and light-blue gauntlet before trading with p2.

I will end the turn. I am drafting a short public message to opponent p4 warning about the pink properties. I am also checking whether p2 is next in turn order.
